# TaxKit documentation

This is the sole router for maintainer-document type, lifecycle, truth layers,
and semantic ownership. Root `README.md` is the public repository entry point;
`AGENTS.md` is the short task map; `docs/architecture/README.md` is the current
architecture route. Public documentation content is a separate product surface
owned by the replacement `apps/web`, backend content contracts and docs
packages. The old `apps/docs` workspace is retired. Its tombstone routes to the verified
source bundle and dated provider recovery records; no provider operation is
authorised by that retained history.

## Truth layers

Use the strongest applicable owner and link rather than copy:

1. External systems own their current external state at readback time.
2. Code, configuration, Schemas, package exports, workflows, and generated
   sources own desired/executable state.
3. Architecture and standards own durable boundaries and enforceable policy.
4. Dated proof/evidence owns one artifact/environment/authority observation and
   its limitations.
5. Active SPEC/tasks and execution plans own current implementation intent.

Provider/registry output cannot grant authority. Completed plans are history.
Local release checks do not prove npm publication or external consumers.

## Metadata and lifecycle

New or materially revised maintainer docs separate `document_type`,
`lifecycle`, `authority`, and `owner`. Current durable docs also record
`last_reviewed` and `review_trigger`; superseded/tombstone docs record a
successor and reason.

Lifecycle values are `proposed`, `current`, `implemented`, `superseded`,
`historical`, `evidence`, `reference`, `failed`, `inconclusive`, `tombstone`,
and `archived`. Authority values are `canonical`, `supporting`, `generated`,
and `external`. Legacy `status: canonical` is an authority marker, not a
lifecycle; migrate it only when its owner is materially revised.

## Routes

| Need | Owner | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture | [`architecture/README.md`](architecture/README.md) | Current architecture route. `architecture.md` is a tombstone only. |
| Standards | [`standards/README.md`](standards/README.md) | Current durable engineering/documentation rules. |
| Current intent | [`product-specs/index.md`](product-specs/index.md) and [`exec-plans/active/README.md`](exec-plans/active/README.md) | Only genuinely active work; implemented/history stays inventory. |
| Completed history | [`exec-plans/completed/README.md`](exec-plans/completed/README.md) | Historical provenance, never default policy. |
| Public docs product | [`../apps/web/README.md`](../apps/web/README.md), [`../packages/docs-content/README.md`](../packages/docs-content/README.md), and [`../packages/docs-fumadocs/README.md`](../packages/docs-fumadocs/README.md) | Consumer-facing content/runtime, not maintainer lifecycle policy. |
| Repeatable release/deployment/recovery operations | [`runbooks/README.md`](runbooks/README.md) and [`operations/authority-model.md`](operations/authority-model.md) | Exactly five target-owned procedures; stop consequential operations when principal, candidate, target or receipt is unknown. |
| CI controls and recurring automation | [`standards/controls.md`](standards/controls.md) and [`operations/automation-register.md`](operations/automation-register.md) | Quality workflow admission, release-graph controls, and report-only candidate boundaries; neither route grants external authority. |
| Verification/critical journeys/proof | [`architecture/testing-and-quality.md`](architecture/testing-and-quality.md), [`verification/critical-journeys.json`](verification/critical-journeys.json), [`evidence/releases/HGI-203-critical-journeys.json`](evidence/releases/HGI-203-critical-journeys.json), [`evidence/releases/HGI-203-local.json`](evidence/releases/HGI-203-local.json), and [`documentation-audit/HGI-203-validation.json`](documentation-audit/HGI-203-validation.json) | The current inventory owns evolving journeys. Accepted HGI-203 retains the exact historical five-journey snapshot and bounded local proof that its immutable packet observed; HGI-204 validates both epochs without attributing current changes to the old attempt. Raw logs and secrets are never durable proof. |
| Harness foundation and requalification | [`verification/repository-harness-profile.json`](verification/repository-harness-profile.json), [`documentation-audit/harness-foundation/accepted-findings.json`](documentation-audit/harness-foundation/accepted-findings.json), [`verification/harness-epochs.md`](verification/harness-epochs.md), and [`verification/effectiveness.md`](verification/effectiveness.md) | The TaxKit profile, accepted HE crosswalk, content-addressed skill receipt and focused gate own the implemented baseline. Last accepted epoch `HFI-004-2026-07-24` qualifies saved candidate `7c8a96e`; HGI-206 remains previous history. The active clean-slate plan owns pending qualification of today's graph. Neither saved epoch establishes current-checkout or external state. |
| References | [`references/README.md`](references/README.md) | Revalidate mutable external guidance. |
| Audit/accounting | [`documentation-audit/README.md`](documentation-audit/README.md) | Dated evidence, not policy. |

Failed/inconclusive work retains provenance, last successful step, observed
state, escalation, resume trigger, recovery, and non-claims outside default
current routes. Do not delete or move historical/public/binary evidence without
an approved retention manifest.

## Maintenance

Every material slice decides `Change required`, `Preserve`, or `N/A` for docs,
READMEs, architecture, standards, public/generated references, runbooks,
proof/evidence, skills, lint/config/CI, and active SPEC/tasks. Update the
earliest durable owner and necessary pointers in the same slice. Counts prove
accounting only; semantic and consumer claims need owner review and
boundary-matched proof.

Use the plugin `development-workflows:docs-maintainer` skill for this impact decision on
both PRD and ordinary changes. `$docs-writer` is limited to public-copy wording
after the maintenance route has selected the owner; it cannot close lifecycle,
generated-content, package, proof, or validation work. Background freshness
scans produce report-only candidates and cannot publish policy or documentation
without separately attached implementation authority, review and publication
identity.

`bun run check:docs` enforces the mechanical owner contract in
[`../tools/documentation/owner-policy.json`](../tools/documentation/owner-policy.json).
It checks maintainer metadata, links, documented commands, workspace README
coverage, public/maintainer separation, accepted public-status representation,
and generated-source edges with bounded diagnostics and a JSON detail receipt.
The command accepts `--json`; failed checks return a nonzero exit after the
report is saved. Effect CLI owns option parsing.
`draft` means authored, locally renderable, visibly labelled candidate content;
`published` means explicitly accepted current public documentation. Neither
status proves runtime or external availability.

Acceptance-record Schemas live in `@taxkit/content`. The docs tool explicitly
selects source exports so it can run in a fresh checkout before package builds.
Version-two records include the reviewed source hash, which this check verifies;
version-one records retain their historical contract. The local accepted
catalogue builder, `bun run docs:catalogue`, requires version two, checks source
bytes before and after compilation, and writes generated output only when
accepted pages and matching navigation exist. It does not accept pages or
establish publication by running. See
[`../packages/docs-content/README.md`](../packages/docs-content/README.md).

`bun run check:runbooks` Schema-decodes the canonical runbook contract, the
current journey inventory and the exact historical HGI-203 journey snapshot,
then reconciles the immutable packet digest, four Markdown owners, commands,
evidence paths, stop operations, index rows and authority rows. It writes only
the ignored bounded receipt `tmp/runbook-validation-report.json`, executes none
of the documented procedures and establishes no consequential state.

Shared development workflows: [latest plugin and repository profiles](skills.md).

# TaxKit documentation

and semantic ownership. Root `README.md` is the public repository entry point;
`AGENTS.md` is the short task map; `docs/architecture/README.md` is the current
architecture route. Public documentation content is a separate product surface
owned by the replacement `apps/web`, backend content contracts and docs
packages. The old `apps/docs` workspace is retired. Its tombstone routes to the verified
source bundle and dated provider recovery records; no provider operation is
authorised by that retained history.

## Truth layers

Use the strongest applicable owner and link rather than copy:

1. External systems own their current external state at readback time.
2. Code, configuration, Schemas, package exports, workflows, and generated
   sources own desired/executable state.
3. Architecture and standards own durable boundaries and enforceable policy.
4. Dated proof/evidence owns one artifact/environment/authority observation and
   its limitations.
5. Active SPEC/tasks and execution plans own current implementation intent.

Provider/registry output cannot grant authority. Completed plans are history.
Local release checks do not prove npm publication or external consumers.

## Metadata and lifecycle

New or materially revised maintainer docs separate `document_type`,
`lifecycle`, `authority`, and `owner`. Current durable docs also record
`last_reviewed` and `review_trigger`; superseded/tombstone docs record a
successor and reason.

Lifecycle values are `proposed`, `current`, `implemented`, `superseded`,
`historical`, `evidence`, `reference`, `failed`, `inconclusive`, `tombstone`,
and `archived`. Authority values are `canonical`, `supporting`, `generated`,
and `external`. Legacy `status: canonical` is an authority marker, not a
lifecycle; migrate it only when its owner is materially revised.

|---|---|---|

accepted pages and matching navigation exist. It does not accept pages or
establish publication by running. See

`bun run check:runbooks` Schema-decodes the canonical runbook contract, the
current journey inventory and the exact historical HGI-203 journey snapshot,
then reconciles the immutable packet digest, four Markdown owners, commands,
evidence paths, stop operations, index rows and authority rows. It writes only
the ignored bounded receipt `tmp/runbook-validation-report.json`, executes none
of the documented procedures and establishes no consequential state.

content.text:
❓ Q5 — Old HTTP helpers: should we replace the public helpers that expose raw clients or create Layers through functions? ➡️ I recommend replacing them with named, checked operations and fixed Layers, then updating the examples together. This follows the strict Effect skill, but callers using those old helpers will need to update their code.
- Replace the old helpers (recommended)
- Keep them temporarily with a stated compatibility exception

❓ Q6 — Website address: should we preserve the API’s current Website-only browser access and Website-specific discovery replies by allowing one checked Website address setting? ➡️ I recommend this narrow exception to Alchemy’s native-address rule. It removes the circular dependency without an Alchemy patch. Following the rule everywhere would instead require moving discovery documents into the Website and changing browser/MCP access rules; Common Practice’s broader MCP rule also uses a separate Effect patch.
- Preserve behaviour; allow the narrow address exception (recommended)
- Use native addresses throughout; review the API changes next

content.text:
1. **Replace the old HTTP helpers?**  
   I recommend named, checked operations and fixed Effect Layers. This follows the strict Effect rules, but existing callers must update. The alternative is keeping the helpers temporarily with a stated exception.

2. **Allow one checked Website address setting?**  
   I recommend this narrow exception to Alchemy’s native-address rule. It preserves current API behaviour and removes the circular dependency without an Alchemy patch. The alternative uses native addresses everywhere, but requires changes to discovery documents and browser/MCP access.

Q5 is recorded: **replace the old helpers and update callers/examples together.**

Common Practice avoids the circular dependency:

- **The Website gets the API’s address and private connection.** Each app gets its own address from Alchemy. The API never needs the Website’s running address. [Declarations](/Users/cooper/Projects/common-practice/apps/web/src/lib/build/cloudflare.ts:202)
- **The API allows browsers from any valid HTTP(S) website**, with credentialed requests disabled. It has no Website-only restriction. [Access rules](/Users/cooper/Projects/common-practice/apps/api/src/http/handler.layer.ts:47)
- **Discovery and canonical links point to the fixed Production website**, including when served from previews. The API still builds those documents. [Canonical links](/Users/cooper/Projects/common-practice/packages/content/src/publication.egress.ts:16)
- **Alchemy is unpatched.** Its broader MCP access rule uses a separate Effect patch. [Patch](/Users/cooper/Projects/common-practice/patches/effect@4.0.2.patch:19)

My earlier recommendation favoured preserving TaxKit’s current behaviour. **To match Common Practice, I’d instead use its one-way setup**, with public browser access and fixed Production canonical links. That removes the need for the Website-address exception.

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

In Default mode, strongly prefer making reasonable assumptions and executing the user's request rather than stopping to ask questions.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.

If explicit user input is required for another reason before progress can safely continue, do not use the `request_user_input` tool. Ask the user directly with one concise plain-text question instead. Never write a multiple choice question as a textual assistant message.

# TaxKit documentation

This is the sole router for maintainer-document type, lifecycle, truth layers,
and semantic ownership. Root `README.md` is the public repository entry point;
`AGENTS.md` is the short task map; `docs/architecture/README.md` is the current
architecture route. Public documentation content is a separate product surface
owned by the replacement `apps/web`, backend content contracts and docs
packages. The old `apps/docs` workspace is retired. Its tombstone routes to the verified
source bundle and dated provider recovery records; no provider operation is
authorised by that retained history.

## Truth layers

Use the strongest applicable owner and link rather than copy:

1. External systems own their current external state at readback time.
2. Code, configuration, Schemas, package exports, workflows, and generated
   sources own desired/executable state.
3. Architecture and standards own durable boundaries and enforceable policy.
4. Dated proof/evidence owns one artifact/environment/authority observation and
   its limitations.
5. Active SPEC/tasks and execution plans own current implementation intent.

Provider/registry output cannot grant authority. Completed plans are history.
Local release checks do not prove npm publication or external consumers.

## Metadata and lifecycle

New or materially revised maintainer docs separate `document_type`,
`lifecycle`, `authority`, and `owner`. Current durable docs also record
`last_reviewed` and `review_trigger`; superseded/tombstone docs record a
successor and reason.

Lifecycle values are `proposed`, `current`, `implemented`, `superseded`,
`historical`, `evidence`, `reference`, `failed`, `inconclusive`, `tombstone`,
and `archived`. Authority values are `canonical`, `supporting`, `generated`,
and `external`. Legacy `status: canonical` is an authority marker, not a
lifecycle; migrate it only when its owner is materially revised.

## Routes

| Need | Owner | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture | [`architecture/README.md`](architecture/README.md) | Current architecture route. `architecture.md` is a tombstone only. |
| Standards | [`standards/README.md`](standards/README.md) | Current durable engineering/documentation rules. |

Failed/inconclusive work retains provenance, last successful step, observed
state, escalation, resume trigger, recovery, and non-claims outside default
current routes. Do not delete or move historical/public/binary evidence without
an approved retention manifest.

## Maintenance

Every material slice decides `Change required`, `Preserve`, or `N/A` for docs,
READMEs, architecture, standards, public/generated references, runbooks,
proof/evidence, skills, lint/config/CI, and active SPEC/tasks. Update the
earliest durable owner and necessary pointers in the same slice. Counts prove
accounting only; semantic and consumer claims need owner review and
boundary-matched proof.

Use the plugin `development-workflows:docs-maintainer` skill for this impact decision on
both PRD and ordinary changes. `$docs-writer` is limited to public-copy wording
after the maintenance route has selected the owner; it cannot close lifecycle,
generated-content, package, proof, or validation work. Background freshness
scans produce report-only candidates and cannot publish policy or documentation
without separately attached implementation authority, review and publication
identity.

`bun run check:docs` enforces the mechanical owner contract in
[`../tools/documentation/owner-policy.json`](../tools/documentation/owner-policy.json).
It checks maintainer metadata, links, documented commands, workspace README
coverage, public/maintainer separation, accepted public-status representation,
and generated-source edges with bounded diagnostics and a JSON detail receipt.
The command accepts `--json`; failed checks return a nonzero exit after the
report is saved. Effect CLI owns option parsing.
`draft` means authored, locally renderable, visibly labelled candidate content;
`published` means explicitly accepted current public documentation. Neither
status proves runtime or external availability.

Acceptance-record Schemas live in `@taxkit/content`. The docs tool explicitly
selects source exports so it can run in a fresh checkout before package builds.
Version-two records include the reviewed source hash, which this check verifies;
version-one records retain their historical contract. The local accepted
catalogue builder, `bun run docs:catalogue`, requires version two, checks source
bytes before and after compilation, and writes generated output only when
accepted pages and matching navigation exist. It does not accept pages or
establish publication by running. See
[`../packages/docs-content/README.md`](../packages/docs-content/README.md).

`bun run check:runbooks` Schema-decodes the canonical runbook contract, the
current journey inventory and the exact historical HGI-203 journey snapshot,
then reconciles the immutable packet digest, four Markdown owners, commands,
evidence paths, stop operations, index rows and authority rows. It writes only
the ignored bounded receipt `tmp/runbook-validation-report.json`, executes none
of the documented procedures and establishes no consequential state.

a9a3eb1eef75a61b1ad89cb6118442847bb2bef2 Record Website RPC verification and deployments
# Architecture

The Website renders Home, About, Contact, the training catalogue, course overviews,
training pages and named missing-page views. A separate API Worker serves the
same checked pages and courses to the Website and agents. Contact has a
form preview with sending disabled; there is no submission service, database or sign-in.

[ADR 0002](docs/adr/0002-api-owned-publishing.md) owns the accepted split and
[the implementation plan](docs/exec-plans/frontend-backend-split.md) records its
checks and delivery. [CONTEXT.md](CONTEXT.md) defines Page and Published page.

## Owners and imports

The [accepted training package decision](docs/adr/0004-training-packages-and-atom-progress.md)
defines `@content/training` and `@common-practice/training`, with native
Atom-managed browser progress. The [implementation ledger](docs/exec-plans/training-course-design.md)
records acceptance and separate release proof. The table describes the implementation.

| Owner                                                         | Responsibility                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `content/pages` — `@content/pages`                            | Authored Markdown files and YAML metadata                                                                                      |
| `content/training` — `@content/training`                      | Authored sample-course outlines and training MDX; server-only source collection                                                |
| `packages/training` — `@common-practice/training`             | Checked course/chapter identities, course service and Layers, immutable course/progress rules                                  |
| `packages/appearance` — `@common-practice/appearance`         | Portable checked appearance choices, browser service, scoped live/test Layers and native Atom actions using a supplied runtime |
| `packages/content` — `@common-practice/content`               | Checked Page, PublishedPage, formats, errors, Content service, live/test Layers, parsing, publication metadata and image cache |
| `packages/http` — `@common-practice/http`                     | Native HTTP contract, handlers, clients, status mapping and shared response headers                                            |
| `packages/rpc` — `@common-practice/rpc`                       | Native RPC contract, handlers and client Layer                                                                                 |
| `packages/mcp` — `@common-practice/mcp`                       | Shared tool definitions/handlers, native remote MCP, resources, prompt and discovery card                                      |
| `packages/analytics` — `@common-practice/analytics`           | Checked capture settings, event vocabulary, closed browser/backend services and bounded native HTTP capture                    |
| `packages/infrastructure` — `@common-practice/infrastructure` | Shared deployment schemas, telemetry stacks, zone ownership, request observation and isolate identity                          |
| `apps/api` — `@common-practice/api`                           | Bundle authored sources, private Takumi renderer, API composition, publishing/discovery routes and native Worker               |
| `apps/web` — `@common-practice/web`                           | TanStack HTML, navigation, page heads, error states, private binding adapter and browser WebMCP host                           |

Each package has explicit source exports and no runtime of its own. Imports
between workspaces use those exports. No package imports an app. The root Bun
catalogs own exact shared versions. All owned code, including tests and
infrastructure, follows the strict Effect skill.

## A page request

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SSR[Website server loader] --> Binding[Private same-stage binding]
  Browser[Browser loader / WebMCP] --> Public[Public API /rpc]
  Binding --> Client[Shared Content and Training RPC clients]
  Public --> Client
  Agent[HTTP / RPC / MCP agent] --> Handler[Shared transport handler]
  Client --> Handler
  Handler --> Content[Content service and live Layer]
  Sources[Bundled authored Markdown] --> Content
  Content --> Image[Checked title sent to private renderer]
```

The API imports raw Markdown and MDX using Alchemy's native `?raw` loader.
The bundled source lists belong to `apps/api/src/sources.ts` and
`apps/api/src/training.sources.ts`; the authored packages export files rather
than unused duplicate inventories. Course outlines remain the only page-order
owner. Content's `live.layer.ts` parses and checks the sources once when the
Layer is built. Invalid
metadata, unsupported Markdown or duplicate identities stop startup with a
named error. No source files are read during a request. The supported body has
one matching top-level heading and an introductory paragraph, followed by
optional second-level sections. Each section has one or more plain text paragraphs,
separated by blank lines, and/or third-level items, each with one plain text
paragraph. Section identifiers are
derived from their headings and checked for uniqueness. Content checks the
structure and text limits; the Website renders those checked sections. The
original Markdown remains the text representation. Legacy single-paragraph
pages and their old placeholder notice remain readable.

Training MDX uses a separate checked reading body. The Content-owned parser reads
a real Markdown/MDX syntax tree and admits prose, headings, simple lists, safe
links, images with alt text, fenced code/prompt blocks and static callouts.
Imports, expressions, executable attributes and arbitrary components reject
startup. It never compiles or executes authored JavaScript. The same checked
blocks feed Website HTML and readable Markdown; transport data includes them.
`Page.reading` is native Option inside the domain; its JSON codec retains an
omitted key or the existing reading array. Markdown output escapes literal
underscores, entities and line-start markers so reparsing preserves their text.

`Content.getPage({ id, format })` is one operation. Omitted `format` means
`data`, a complete PublishedPage with content, Markdown/image addresses and
search metadata. Explicit `markdown`, `og` and `seo` formats return those views.
Every response repeats `format`. Literal/default inputs have exact types;
a runtime choice returns a union that narrows when its `format` is checked.
One small schema-selected operation adapter is shared by both clients and
Content; it checks that the returned variant matches the request.

Schemas, derived types and named errors belong to Content. HTTP, RPC and MCP
reuse them. The native builders validate requests and encode outputs. Image
bytes use Effect's base64 codec on JSON transports and decode to checked PNG
bytes in typed clients. Expected errors decode to native tagged Effect errors.
A transport failure and an invalid response have separate named errors.

Both Content clients allow 40 seconds for each complete read, including the
reply body. Content owns this shared deadline. It leaves ten seconds beyond
the API's 30-second image limit for sending and checking the reply. Expiry
interrupts the pending call and returns the existing `ContentUnavailableError`
with its operation name; earlier caller cancellation stays interruption.
There is no automatic client retry.

Content reads a page once and passes a small checked title to its image service.
That service never calls Content. Its live Layer exposes the same service to
other checked publications. It owns a two-key, five-minute success cache, one
render permit and a 30-second timeout; failures expire immediately. The default
page response advertises the image address without rendering it. The API's
private Takumi adapter owns image SDK Promise calls. Browser PostHog calls stay
in the Website's private analytics adapter; backend capture uses native Effect
HttpClient rather than another SDK or Promise runner.

## Runtime and frontend loading

Owned Layers are static values. Their Requirements type channel names the
services they need, including authored sources, test fixtures, checked addresses
and shared browser settings. Callers supply these through native `Layer.succeed`;
tests replace implementations with native Effect Layers. Host configuration
still belongs to Effect Config. Declaring a Layer does not acquire its resources;
the existing runtime and scopes keep their current lifetimes. The
[lint policy](docs/standards/lint.md#static-layers) records enforcement and limits.

`apps/api/src/deployment/cloudflare/worker.ts` uses Alchemy's native Worker
class-and-`make` pattern. The lightweight class keeps the renderer and server
implementation out of Website bindings. Its native runtime builds Content,
Training, images and routes once per isolate. TrainingLive validates the authored
outlines against that same Content service. `apps/api/src/application.layer.ts` checks
the API address and builds the native handler in Alchemy's instance Scope.
Shared services stay alive until that instance stops. Each request runs in its incoming Effect
fibre with its own cancellation, tracer and Scope. Streamed responses retain
that Scope until completion or cancellation. There is no API ManagedRuntime
or extra Promise runner.

The MCP route Layer reads and checks `COMMON_PRACTICE_API_URL` through Effect
Config once during startup. Alchemy supplies this setting from native
`Cloudflare.Worker.URL`. The page template and discovery card share that checked
address through the `ApiIdentity` requirement. No incoming request is needed
for registration.

Native Alchemy planning registers that Worker and its telemetry. It skips runtime
binding reads because Alchemy resolves `Worker.URL` only before upload. The native
`globalThis.__ALCHEMY_RUNTIME__` build flag removes deployment-only settings from
the uploaded bundle, so startup never asks for stack-only Stage or Zone services.
The native
`ALCHEMY_PHASE` selects startup of the real application after Alchemy supplies the
running Worker's checked bindings. Source validation and native bundle tests are
local proof; the public suite checks the uploaded application.

The Website keeps one server runtime at `apps/web/src/lib/runtime.server.ts`.
Every TanStack server entry point uses its one runner. Loader cancellation
combines the incoming request signal and the router signal.
`api/binding.adapter.layer.ts` checks the host binding against the methods needed
by Alchemy, using the binding type derived from the Website declaration. Its
Schema preserves the original host object so `fetch` keeps its receiver. It uses Alchemy's public
`fromCloudflareFetcher` and `toHttpClient` adapters from the published
`alchemy/Cloudflare/Bridge` runtime entry. Alchemy owns Promise
conversion, cancellation and its bounded handler-not-ready retry. It clones
the request per attempt and preserves streamed replies. The native HTTP carrier
serves shared Effect RPC clients at `/rpc`; those clients provide the existing
Content and Training contracts to page loaders. Web Request/Response
conversion for TanStack stays in the single server runtime. There is no local
backend fallback and no Effect Context passed through TanStack.

The host ingress selects the four application settings once and supplies a native
Effect ConfigProvider through Alchemy's protected-binding adapter. The same provider
feeds the existing `WebsiteAppConfig` and deployment-stage declarations, which own
their Schema checks. The configuration reader accepts that provider without
redeclaring the settings as unchecked fields. This happens when the existing runtime
first builds its Layer. It keeps the checked settings or the existing named error for that
Layer's lifetime. Invalid public settings still produce the unavailable loader
result; they do not prevent the private Content client from forwarding requests.

`seo/page.loader.ts` uses local TanStack server/client environment functions.
There are no Website `createServerFn` wrappers, including for settings, and no
Website `/rpc` proxy. Server loaders await private RPC before rendering complete
page content and metadata. Browser loaders use request atoms in the existing
Atom runtime; its sole loader bridge waits through `AtomRegistry.getResult`
and carries the router cancellation signal. A retained resource atom owns the
shared RPC clients; per-request atoms own individual cancellation. Root
configuration is local setup: server cookies and checked bindings become
encoded root data, then browser reloads use that data and live appearance.

Page loaders encode the complete checked success/error envelope. This preserves error tags
through TanStack's JSON serialisation, instead of throwing an error whose useful
fields would be lost. Routes render returned page text and metadata, or a named
error state. Training's narrow synchronous React receiver checks each changed
encoded loader reply once, restoring native Option and error values or returning
a named invalid-response error. It creates no runtime. The Website has no authored
page records or image renderer.

The browser has one Effect Atom runtime in `runtime.client.ts`. The router
creates its registry before loaders run; React uses that same registry through
RegistryContext and disposes it at final root unmount. Native Atom React
scheduling cancels pending disposal during development mount replay. SSR uses
an isolated RegistryProvider. The registry is local router context, never an
Effect Context or serialised loader data. Checked Website/API addresses from
the root server loader initialise retained configuration atoms. The browser
uses shared Effect RPC clients at the public API `/rpc`, over native
FetchHttpClient with no credentials and no redirects, and shared tool handlers. Unmounting
closes the tool registration Scope. `browser-atom.ts` reaches this runtime only
inside TanStack's client environment function; server rendering mounts an inert
Atom. No browser global is read during import.

Appearance's checked choices, branded options, cookie readers/writers, browser
service and native Atom model belong to `@common-practice/appearance`. That
source-only package depends on Effect only. Its manifest and TypeScript settings
can be copied without repository catalogs or app configuration. It imports no
app, other workspace package, React, TanStack, Alchemy, artwork or CSS. The
Website's `appearance/settings.ts` supplies its existing cookie/channel names
and `appearance` attribute, preserving previously saved choices. The Website
owns colours, footer layout, server adaptation and cache policy. See the
[package guide](packages/appearance/README.md) for its public API and copy setup.

The Website's `AppearanceFavicon` reads that same checked choice from the root
registry. React owns its single icon link in the document head, including the
server render seeded from the cookie. `appearance/favicon.ts` maps choices to
Schema-branded asset paths: fixed Navy for Light, fixed Bone for Dark, and the
device-responsive SVG for Use device setting. The three assets retain the exact
original symbol path and dimensions. This adds no runtime, host mutation or
favicon responsibility to the reusable package.

Cookie readers accept the Schema-branded `AppearanceCookieHeader`, checked at
the Website/server or browser host boundary. Empty and malformed preferences
keep their device fallback; invalid header control characters are rejected.
The Website's `appearance/input.ingress.ts` owns the dropdown input Schema and
decoder. Its input Atom in the existing runtime decodes before calling the
package's checked `change` operation. The package exposes no raw-input action:
both `setChoice` and `change` accept the shared `AppearanceRequest` Schema type.
Server-side inert Atoms reuse those same Schema-derived types.

Appearance uses this same runtime and registry. Only its Layer is part of the
base browser runtime. Training components reach progress through their own
client environment adapter; each course acquires its supplied storage Layer
inside its resource Atom on the first restore or action. Both local features
work independently of remote configuration. One private Atom
checks and shares remote configuration without starting remote services.
Analytics has its own scoped services Atom, acquired by page views, navigation
and learning events and retained until the root registry closes. WebMCP's
registration Atom acquires only its host and tool-handler Layers; unmounting
closes those Layers and unregisters its tools. Neither service starts the other.
Missing remote settings cannot prevent local settings or progress working.
The root loader reads a Schema-checked, host-only appearance cookie through the
existing server runtime. HTML and the root registry receive the same starting
choice. CSS follows device appearance without an early script or another runner.
The package's private browser appearance adapter checks cookie writes by reading them
back. BroadcastChannel notifications and focus checks refresh the checked saved
choice; their listeners and channel close with the root registry. A blocked save
keeps the current visit's choice and shows a footer notice. This cookie is
separate from training progress and carries no identifiers or analytics data.

The package exposes named Light, Dark, device, toggle and checked-choice actions.
One semaphore orders all changes. State is read-only to callers; new changes
use those actions or their typed Effect programs. The device and resolved
appearance use Option until a real device reading is available, so a toggle
cannot silently guess. Device events update the resolved Atom even while an
explicit choice remains fixed. Native resources close with the supplied root
registry. Only its exact contract test constructs isolated test runtimes;
production package code never constructs a runtime.

The WebMCP host adapter registers only when the browser's exact origin matches
the deployed Website's checked self address. This includes its matching Preview
and local address. Remote MCP has a separate public Origin policy.

The only command runtimes are `tools/references/sync.runtime.ts` and
`tools/checks/docs.runtime.ts`. Tests run through `@effect/vitest`. Host Promise
exceptions are limited to the Website runner, its Cloudflare service-binding
adapter, the private Takumi adapter, the browser WebMCP host and the private
browser analytics adapter. PostHog's synchronous before-send callback is an
exact consumer: it returns a checked event containing only allowed fields, or
null. It never runs another Effect runtime.

The root head preloads the self-hosted Latin normal Literata file used by page
headings. A page head also preloads Latin italic when its heading has emphasis,
including the training catalogue's opening heading. Course outlines and lessons
use normal headings and do not preload italic. Vite resolves both URLs from
the same font files used by CSS, with anonymous cross-origin font requests.
`seo/font-links.ts` constructs both descriptors through one Effect Schema with
fixed literal defaults. Page heads use native Option and Array helpers to include
the italic link, and Struct.evolve to append the alternate representation link.
Other font subsets and Geist Mono remain demand
loaded by CSS. TanStack retains its native route component splitting.

Owned `Effect.promise` and `Effect.tryPromise` calls are limited to the exact
Website runner, Takumi, WebMCP and browser analytics adapter files. Only the
existing WebMCP host-contract test may also use `Effect.promise`. The service
binding uses Alchemy's native conversion and needs no owned Promise bridge.
The lint policy enforces these exact files, SDK value imports and Website
Cloudflare binding access, including dynamic imports and aliases.

### Host settings

The host supplies settings through its existing Effect ConfigProvider or an
adapter that reads only the app's named settings. The Layer that uses a fixed
setting reads and checks it with the owning Schema during startup. Use
`Layer.effect` to build an existing service,
or `Layer.unwrap` to configure existing Layers, as MCP does. Keep operations
using the checked value for that Layer's lifetime. This also applies to feature
switches, limits, timeouts and private credentials; preserve redaction for secrets.

Native Alchemy Workers supply Effect's ConfigProvider from their bindings.
For an explicitly declared runtime binding, `Config.schema` reads and checks
its value in one step. Self addresses are explicitly bound with
`Cloudflare.Worker.URL`, then read after Alchemy resolves them before upload.

Reusable settings have a named Config declaration in their owner's `config.ts`.
`@common-practice/http/config` exports `ApiOriginConfig` for both the API
application and MCP Layer. The declaration combines the owning Schema and key;
it stays lazy until yielded during startup.

| Declaration             | Owner and use                                                                                       |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ApiOriginConfig`       | HTTP owns the API's checked address; the API, MCP and Website reuse it.                             |
| `DeploymentStageConfig` | Infrastructure owns the runtime stage; the API and Website reuse it.                                |
| `PostHogCaptureConfig`  | Analytics owns the checked capture JSON and its disabled fallback.                                  |
| `WorkerAnalyticsConfig` | Infrastructure combines stage and capture settings, preserving the complete `CaptureBinding` check. |
| `WebsiteAppConfig`      | The Website combines the shared API address and capture settings with its own checked address.      |

The Website's narrow host adapter supplies only its named settings through
`ConfigProvider.fromUnknown` and Alchemy's native `reifyBoundConfigProvider`.
That helper handles both ordinary bindings and Alchemy's protected format;
application code does not maintain a second decoder for that format.

Effect Schema's native URL codec checks the Website's self URL before its origin
is constructed with the owning branded Schema. Credentials, paths, queries and
fragments are rejected; a root slash is allowed on Alchemy's self URL. The shared
API origin remains a strict serialised origin. Config recipes reuse the existing
Schemas, their brands and their complete record checks. Related settings use
`Config.all`; they do not need another Context service.

Required API addresses and stages have no default. Invalid values fail native
startup. Website address failures and missing or invalid stages return the
existing unavailable configuration result; stage errors have no disabled fallback.
Missing, malformed or differently staged capture settings disable analytics.
`Config.withDefault` and `Config.option` handle missing input; deliberate
recovery from invalid optional analytics uses `Config.orElse`. Each runtime
keeps its settings until its Layer is rebuilt. Fixed protocol implementations
and address validity rules remain code; an environment key is added only for a
real deployment choice.

Host Layers yield Config directly to read fixed deployment settings. They pass
the resulting checked values to static reusable Layers through named Context
requirements, such as `ApiIdentity`, `HttpApiAddress` and `AnalyticsSettings`.
These requirements allow callers and tests to replace the inputs using native
Layers; they add no second configuration reader. Ordinary checked helper inputs
stay typed arguments. Current request data comes from the native request service
inside a handler; it does not choose the server's startup address. Tests provide
their own ConfigProvider at the host edge. Browser code receives only checked
public settings through the existing root loader and browser runtime.

robots, sitemap, llms and well-known discovery paths before HTML routing, so local
and built responses use the same API output. Existing file handlers still declare

routes are removed without aliases or redirects.

## Training and browser progress

`@content/training` contains three sample courses, each with three chapters and
two pages per chapter. One outline owns each course's page order. MDX owns titles
and bodies. Training owns course/chapter brands and reuses Content's PageId;
Content never imports Training. Missing, duplicate, unlisted or incorrectly
addressed pages stop TrainingLive construction. HTTP, RPC and both MCP surfaces
reuse `listCourses` and `getCourse`; all bodies use the single Content.getPage
operation. Discovery publishes the catalogue, course hierarchy and all pages.
Training's publication export owns catalogue/course metadata and checked image
inputs, using Content's generic publication helper. Their heads reuse the
Website's complete canonical, JSON-LD, OG and Twitter fields. Dedicated title
cards use the API's existing Takumi renderer and shared image cache.

The Website checks course, chapter and slug inputs in its existing server
function owner. Course and page loaders return checked success/error envelopes,
preserving named failures through TanStack serialisation. Public course/page
HTML is independent of saved progress and available before browser code loads.
Training owns separate total/completed page and chapter count brands, reused by
summaries, progress and analytics. Pure calculated totals return native Result
with a named count error; invalid bounds or inconsistent completion fail checking.

Training's `progress-atoms` export accepts the existing Website Atom runtime
and an Atom containing its storage Layer. The kept-alive resource Atom builds
that Layer in its own Scope only when restoration or an action needs it.
It creates no runtime, registry or second progress service. One writable native
Atom per course owns progress and load/save status. Runtime atom/fn operations
use KeyValueStore.toSchemaStore with CourseProgress's native JSON codec. A
per-course semaphore restores once before any action and orders saves. Browser
storage acquisition is checked in the Website's narrow storage adapter.

Missing records start fresh. Invalid records start fresh with a notice; blocked
storage and failed saves retain progress in memory with an accessible notice.
Controls wait for restoration. Kept-alive action atoms survive route changes;
closing React's root registry interrupts pending work. One versioned key per
course isolates resets. Tabs use last-write-wins records and can remain stale
until reload. There is no merge engine, cross-device sync or offline promise.

Pure rules calculate visits, completion/undo, reset, resume and current totals.
Stable existing page IDs survive edits; removed IDs do not contribute and new
pages start incomplete. Free page jumps and previous/next links never complete
pages. Explicit completion advances; the final page returns to a summary with
review links. A reset asks for confirmation for that course.

HTTP and RPC are public read-only APIs with credential-free CORS. The API allows
native Effect's `b3` and `traceparent` request headers, so the browser Content
client can read pages without disabling tracing. Remote MCP is anonymous and
broadly accessible to compatible agents, including valid
third-party browser origins. Its native transport supports the published
`2026-07-28` protocol. It accepts absent Origin or a valid serialised HTTP(S)
origin and rejects malformed or opaque origins before CORS, including preflight
requests. A small pinned Effect patch lets the existing native Origin check use
a checked predicate; no transport validation is bypassed. Compatibility and
connect/list/call behaviour require their own public checks.

The [accepted follow-up design](docs/standards/dependencies.md#removing-the-effect-and-posthog-patches)
will move that check into the existing API host, then remove only the checked
Origin from the request passed to unchanged native MCP. Implementation is pending;
the current patch remains in use.

## Joint deployment

`alchemy.run.ts` composes native Cloudflare/GitHub providers and Cloudflare-backed
state for the `common-practice` stack. Checked stages are `dev`, `preview`, `integration`,
`production` and `pr-<number>`. It deploys both apps together and returns checked
Website/API addresses as native stack outputs after Schema checks. The API
address feeds the Website binding through native `Output.mapEffect`, so Alchemy
can recognise an unchanged address while planning. An Action output would stay
unresolved and make that binding appear changed on every plan.
The Website address also uses native `Output.mapEffect`. Both checks run when
Alchemy resolves the output, and retain their named validation failures. The
Website check no longer saves an Action result that could skip changed
validation code. The deployment runbook covers removal of its old saved record.

All root stacks share `@common-practice/infrastructure/secrets`: native
`Doppler.Secrets`, then `Alchemy.Secrets.DotEnv`, with `ProcessEnv` disabled.
The optional ignored `.env` overrides Doppler in local and hosted runs alike.
`dev` selects `common-practice/dev`, `production` selects `prd`, and the other
checked stages select `stg_preview`. The production-only telemetry and analytics
stacks use `prd`. Settings stay in Alchemy's ConfigProvider; they are not copied
into the shell or forwarded as a complete Worker environment. Native provider
sign-in still reads `DOPPLER_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `CI` and profile selection
from the real runner environment. CI uses existing read-only config-scoped
Doppler service tokens; it needs no Team-plan identity or OIDC exchange.

The Website stays a standard native `Cloudflare.Website.Vite`. Production retains
`common-practice-production`. The Common Practice cutover declaration makes
`withcommonpractice.com` canonical, with its `www`, the old
`departmentofagenticwork.com` apex and old `www` permanently redirecting to it.
Native Alchemy preserves path and query on those redirects. Both verified zones
keep separate retained resources; the legacy zone records use `CommonPracticeLegacy*` with native former-id declarations; the registered domain is unchanged.
Every hosted Preview stage owns an ordinary Alchemy Website Worker named
`common-practice-<stage>`, with its own code, assets, bindings and native log/trace
settings. It does not reference production's Worker or upload a rollout version.
Non-production Websites use the native `Preview` resource namespace, separating
their identity from the former Worker Preview. Production retains `Website`.
Production serves its custom domains only, with native `workersDev: false`.
Other Websites keep their own stable workers.dev address and disable extra
version-preview addresses. PR URLs do not depend on production's setting.
The Website's existing response policy adds `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` outside
production, using the checked stage and blocking indexing if stage validation
fails. Cloudflare's native `_headers` file applies the same header to static
assets on workers.dev. Production's custom domain remains indexable.

The API retains logical resource `Backend` and physical name
`common-practice-<stage>-backend`. Every stage owns an independent API Worker. Production
declares `api.withcommonpractice.com` as primary and keeps
`api.departmentofagenticwork.com` serving the same Worker as an alias. API requests
are not redirected, so existing RPC and MCP POST clients keep working. Native
Alchemy resolves each exact hostname's own zone; a shared zone override is unsafe
across the two zones. Other hosted stages expose their own workers.dev address. Destroying
a Preview stage removes only its Website Worker and matching API.

Public content, canonical metadata and AI discovery use Common Practice and the
new website origin. Agent discovery lists `common-practice-website`; the former
`daw-website/SKILL.md` URL permanently redirects to the current skill on the same-stage API. Public MCP
identifies as `common-practice`, while its tool and prompt names stay stable.
Telemetry event names, runtime bindings, package names and stack identifiers stay
stable. The production trace filter includes both website origins to preserve
old traffic in the existing dashboards. These are source declarations; the
cutover checklist and dated evidence record deployment separately.

Native development runs Website port 3210 and API port 3211, both strict.
It needs the existing Doppler development credentials for Alchemy's state.
There is no single-app `dev:ui` fallback. The Website's native build hash includes
shared packages, content sources, API sources and the lockfile, so content-only
changes rebuild its version and refresh its cache.

The compatibility date is `2026-09-22`, with `nodejs_compat` and
`enable_request_signal`. Website bindings are explicitly `COMMON_PRACTICE_STAGE`, `BACKEND`,
`COMMON_PRACTICE_API_URL`, `COMMON_PRACTICE_WEBSITE_URL` and checked `COMMON_PRACTICE_POSTHOG_CONFIG`, with no Axiom exporter credentials.
The API binds its checked stage, native self URL and analytics settings. Preview never points at production's API. Deployment
credentials never become Worker bindings.

Shared zone, TLS, DNSSEC and crawler policy owners live in
`@common-practice/infrastructure`. The separate production-only `common-practice-observability` and
`common-practice-trace-export` stacks use Common Practice names, shared Axiom outputs and
removal rules. This app split does not change their resources or dashboards.
Only native Alchemy may plan, apply or destroy. The
[deployment runbook](docs/runbooks/deployment.md) owns those procedures.

## Observability

`@common-practice/analytics` owns checked settings, capture events and the two
closed Effect services. The browser service is private to
`apps/web/src/lib/analytics/browser.adapter.layer.ts`, inside the existing Atom
runtime. It acquires the supported `posthog-js/dist/module.slim.no-external`
build automatically on enabled deployments, only at
the matching Website origin without Do Not Track. There is no consent UI,
stored choice or consent operation. The adapter removes the old Common Practice choice key
and clears any SDK opt-out left by the former controls without an opt-in event.
It disables automatic
capture, recordings, flags, surveys and person profiles. Its synchronous consumer
strips SDK metadata, full URLs, session IDs and person fields. Page and navigation
capture and deliberate learning events share an Effect semaphore. Consecutive
duplicate page views compare the full checked course/chapter/page identities.
Scope closes the client on React unmount. Acquisition failure leaves the service
usable with capture off, preserving page loading and WebMCP.

The checked vocabulary includes course starts, deliberate resumes, explicit page
completion/undo, transitions to all current pages complete and confirmed resets.
Website coordination records these after the progress change; rendering,
restoration and visits do not emit completion events. Capture failure cannot
undo progress or block reading. Fields contain branded identities and bounded
counts owned by Training, never prose, prompts or the saved record. Page views
use closed page alternatives: course views require a course ID, reader views
require all three IDs, and ordinary views forbid them. Existing anonymous identity,
stage separation and relay apply; no new provider resources or dashboards are
added. Attempted capture is separate from proof of stored events.

The SDK sends its selected batches to the checked browser path `/ingest/e/`.
The Website's private `analytics/relay/live.layer.ts` forwards each attempt
once to fixed `https://us.i.posthog.com/e/` through native Effect HttpClient.
`runtime.server.ts` composes it in the existing runtime; the reserved TanStack
route uses that runtime's single runner. The boundary checks the deployment,
exact Website origin, path, method, query and media type. It preserves opaque
batch bytes, caps both bodies at 1 MiB and gives all body/delivery work five
seconds. Scope releases work on failure or cancellation. Redirects are refused;
cookies, caller trace fields, visitor IP headers and authorisation are excluded.
Checked upstream statuses are returned with `no-store`, without Website retries
or direct fallback. The browser keeps its normal batching and retries; loss is
still possible. This route is `analytics-relay` request telemetry, independent
of Content reads and API usage. Assets, remote configuration, flags and replay
have no relay routes. Backend capture keeps its direct host.

The relay's schemas, errors and contract have separate owners. `request.ingress.ts`
checks HTTP input, `response.egress.ts` maps the checked reply, and the shared
`body.ingress.ts` uses native `Stream.limitBytes`, failing when the limit is exceeded.
Optional query fields become `Option` values at ingress and are encoded only
when sending the upstream request.

The API decorates its one Content service to collect completed reads through
HTTP, RPC, MCP and publishing, including failed reads. A request holds at most
64 reads, adds one request-completed event, and schedules one batch through
native Alchemy `WorkerExecutionContext.waitUntil`. Streaming responses complete
their batch when the body closes. Health and preflight requests are skipped.
The native HttpClient sender has a five-second timeout and no retry or queue.
Request IDs are independent of browser visitor IDs. There are no request bodies,
raw paths, full queries, headers or raw IP fields in the capture vocabulary.

`alchemy.posthog.run.ts` owns `common-practice-analytics` at stage `production`: two projects
(Common Practice production and Common Practice preview), four private dashboards, twelve insights and
twelve tiles. Its private Distilled
adapter performs management operations and checks every response. Exact markers
prevent adopting unrelated objects; all lookup pages are read before recovery.
Projects retain event history and refuse replacement. Removing child declarations
soft-deletes only their owned dashboard, insight or tile. App deployment references
the project's redacted public capture key, never the management credential.
The stack's returned project, dashboard and insight counts come from its
environment and dashboard definitions, so adding a declaration updates the count.

The [accepted dashboard follow-up](docs/adr/0003-posthog-project-retention.md#dashboard-update-method--7-october-2026)
will use Distilled's built-in PUT update inside the same Alchemy Provider,
replacing the dashboard PATCH patch after preservation checks. Implementation
is pending.

Production binds the production project. `COMMON_PRACTICE_POSTHOG_TEST=true` opts a hosted
test stage into Common Practice preview; ordinary Previews and all local development
remain disabled. The Preview project's existing `TestProject` logical ID,
`test` ownership markers and capture environment stay stable; changing its
display name updates the same project and preserves its history. The settings
schema rejects a production/test stage mismatch.
Explicit capture env props use Alchemy's native protected-value packing, so
the API's Config provider receives the encoded settings as a string. The Website's
host adapter uses the same native unwrapping before yielding shared checked
Config. Both hosts reuse `WorkerAnalyticsConfig` to disable collection when the
capture settings do not match their runtime stage.
Backend capture and browser page views have separate dashboards.

`Http.observeHostedRequest` writes one Schema-checked `common-practice.request`
record when a response is ready, fails or is cancelled. Each record identifies
Website or backend and contains bounded route, result and traffic categories.
The observer never reads or replaces a response body and records no URL, raw user
agent, credentials or request body. Invalid records emit a fixed warning only.

Both hosts use Effect's JSON console logger. Cloudflare captures those logs and
exports them and native traces to Axiom through separate Alchemy-owned
`ObservabilityDestination` resources. Both signals have explicit sampling rate 1,
persistence enabled and destinations attached on each Worker and Preview. Axiom
is the main investigation store; Cloudflare retains another searchable copy.
The API registers its logger through native `Alchemy.Telemetry.layer` alongside
`Cloudflare.Telemetry()`. Website logging belongs to its existing ManagedRuntime;
the Website uses Cloudflare's automatic request and fetch spans, without an owned
span adapter. Following Alchemy's TanStack example, `api/cloudflare.ingress.ts`
imports `cloudflare:workers` normally and reads `env` inside Effect operations,
not at module evaluation. Host-independent adapters are tested without loading the Cloudflare module. No native Effect
Context is passed through TanStack. `binding.adapter.layer.ts` retains the narrow
host-independent validation and Alchemy-native service-binding adaptation; the existing
WebsiteApi service supplies the checked stage as well as forwarding and configuration.

Neither Worker binds Axiom exporter credentials or runs log/metric uploads. There
is no Website telemetry completion service, monitoring-only Scope or `waitUntil`
adapter. Ordinary application resource and streaming lifetimes remain intact.
Backend PostHog delivery still uses native Alchemy background work; this is a
separate analytics contract. Platform delivery is best effort, never awaited by
application request handling. The hard cutover has no dual-write fallback.

Custom metrics have been removed from both Workers. Existing shared metric data
remains with its owner. Website count charts read the new Cloudflare-delivered
request logs; backend records remain separate. These counts exclude requests
served without executing that Worker and are not browser page views. The five
Axiom dashboards keep their identities; Telemetry Health compares log and trace
coverage and delivery delay rather than custom counters. Shared query readers
must match the observed Cloudflare envelope.

`IsolateIdentity` uses Effect Crypto, Clock and Ref during the first request to
provide an isolate id, request sequence and age. Request logs carry these labels; dashboard queries correlate them to automatic
Website root spans by trace id, identifying first requests without assuming slow means cold. Identity
failure never stops the request. No custom duration is calculated with the frozen
Workers clock. Native CPU time and automatic fetch spans are diagnostic measures;
browser/synthetic timings measure visitor latency. Root span duration may include
background work and is not automatically response time.

The [observability plan](docs/exec-plans/observability.md) owns the approved cutover,
resource ownership and proof requirements. Local checks, Preview deployment,
stored Axiom records, dashboards and production release are separate claims.

## Caching

The Website's TanStack router preloads links on hover, focus or touch and treats
loaded and preloaded page data as fresh for one minute. Returning to the same
page during that minute reuses its loader data without another page-data
request. Unused data keeps TanStack's default five-minute retention window.
After freshness expires, a return can display the saved data while checking
for an update. A full reload starts a new router cache. These settings live in
`apps/web/src/router.tsx`, not Vite's build configuration.

The minute starts when the loader data was produced. Cloudflare-cached HTML
includes the server's saved loader time, so the first return to the initial
page can need a refresh even soon after opening the Website. That new browser
load starts its own freshness window.

The router's memory cache is separate from HTTP caching below. TanStack server
function replies remain `no-store`; the router can still reuse their returned
data. A returned error envelope is also loader data and can be reused during
the same minute. Browser analytics sends have their own lifecycle.

`@common-practice/http/publishing-policy` supplies the shared cache and safety headers and
API-catalogue Link. It is a pure function over response facts. Both native API
responses and TanStack responses use it; failures and cookie-setting responses
stay `no-store`.

The Website uses native Workers Cache scoped to its Worker version. Successful
anonymous HTML, public Markdown and images make browsers recheck (`max-age=0`), while
Cloudflare may reuse them for seven days. Discovery text and the MCP card have
a five-minute browser lifetime. `Vary: Accept` separates HTML and Markdown
negotiation. Public page API successes follow the same headers; API-catalogue,
OpenAPI, RPC, MCP and failures remain `no-store`. The API does not declare native
Workers Cache; its HTTP headers and isolate image cache have separate roles.
Static assets use Cloudflare's asset cache.

TanStack HTML additionally varies on the complete request Cookie header, so an
anonymous cached response cannot match a saved-appearance request. Responses
with the appearance cookie, including malformed values, use `private, no-store`
and CDN `no-store`. Other cookies can reduce anonymous HTML cache reuse. The
independent machine representations and assets keep their existing rules.
Native Workers Cache lookup isolation still needs separate hosted Preview proof.

Shared responses still require identical public content for every visitor.
Change this policy before adding sign-in, other personal content or data that
changes without deployment.
Local checks, hosted cache hits, browser behaviour and provider state remain
separate evidence. Dated records in `docs/evidence` never override this design.
# Website RPC data loading

Status: implemented, verified and deployed to Preview and production,
11 October 2026. The [delivery record](../evidence/publishing/2026-10-11-website-rpc.md)
separates local, browser, provider and public checks. Plugin publication and
pre-existing Preview binding cleanup remain separate items.

[Architecture](../../ARCHITECTURE.md) and
[ADR 0002](../adr/0002-api-owned-publishing.md) own the implemented design.
The completed [Website/API split](frontend-backend-split.md) retains its history.

## Accepted design

Remove every Website `createServerFn` wrapper, including settings. TanStack owns
routes, rendering and navigation. Local isomorphic loader branches select the
existing server runner or browser Atom runtime. Website backend reads share
Effect RPC declarations and Content/Training Schemas and errors. Public HTTP,
RPC and MCP APIs remain available.

```text
first HTML -> server loader -> existing runner -> private BACKEND /rpc
navigation/preload -> client loader -> existing Atom registry/runtime
                   -> checked public API /rpc
root setup -> Website cookie + checked bindings -> encoded initial data
           -> retained browser settings + live appearance
```

Server rendering waits for page text and metadata. Encoded success/error
results preserve named failures and response statuses. Browser data consumers
restore checked values as needed. There is no Website RPC proxy or settings RPC.

The [Alchemy example](https://alchemy.run/cloudflare/frontend/full-stack-tanstack-rpc-drizzle/)
uses a proxy and AtomRpc.Service. This project instead reuses its existing
browser runtime and direct public API, checked against Effect 4.0.2 and Alchemy
2.0.0-beta.81. Those examples do not require changing the site's first render.

## Runtime and cancellation

The router creates a local browser registry before loaders; React uses that same
registry and releases it on final unmount. Development mount replay cancels a
scheduled disposal through Atom React's native scheduler. SSR uses its own
isolated registry. No Effect Context or registry is serialised into loader data.

Hydrated configuration atoms stay alive until registry disposal. A shared
resource atom builds the native RPC services in its Scope. Per-request atoms
let a cancelled navigation stop its own request without closing shared clients.
The sole browser loader bridge waits with AtomRegistry.getResult. Server
loaders combine router and incoming request cancellation. Appearance, progress,
analytics and WebMCP retain their separate acquisition rules in one runtime.

## Contracts and enforcement

Native NDJSON is used on both ends. Semantic client Layers provide Content and
Training; their generated client remains private. The checked getPage operation
retains exact format results and the complete default data response. Total-read
deadlines cover headers and body. Invalid native reply decoding uses a private
marker so an unrelated SchemaError defect is not rewritten as an expected error.

Canonical Commonplace guidance, starter and portable Oxlint checks are updated
together. Common Practice retains the exact portable rule bytes and hashes.
Real negative fixtures cover renamed imports, re-exports, alternate HTTP data
clients, extra runtimes and unguarded runtime calls. Positive fixtures retain
matching environment calls and ordinary HttpClient work.

## Qualification and delivery

- Reference sync: Effect 4.0.2 and Alchemy 2.0.0-beta.81 verified against the lock.
- Focused native RPC tests cover complete pages, all four formats, image bytes,
  courses, all six Content failures and all four Training failures.
- Browser registry tests cover retained settings, shared transport, interruption
  and final cleanup; analytics acquisition remains independent.
- A real React StrictMode probe mounted the actual BrowserRegistry component:
  replay mounted twice and cleaned up once while keeping one acquired client
  alive. Final unmount disposed the registry once and released the client once.
- The actual browser loader bridge received an AbortController signal while
  its native GetPage request was paused. Aborting rejected the wait with Effect
  interruption and Chrome reported `net::ERR_ABORTED`, `canceled: true` for
  that same request. Temporary interception and the probe registry were removed.
- Local browser navigation showed direct API `/rpc/` POSTs and successful CORS.
  Training and existing saved progress rendered; WebMCP tools registered at the
  matching Website origin.
  Calling WebMCP get_page for Home SEO returned the checked variant through
  the same public RPC client. Dark appearance survived reload; the prior Light
  choice was then restored and all existing course progress remained unchanged.
- Hovering About made one direct GetPage request; clicking and returning with
  forward navigation within the existing 60-second window reused that result.
  Returning again after 78 seconds made a new GetPage request and rendered it.
- The hosted public suite against local development passed seven of eight
  tests, covering page bodies/metadata, HTTP/RPC/MCP, discovery and errors. The
  remaining assertion expects Cloudflare's static `noindex` header on the
  favicon, which Vite does not supply. Hosted Preview passed that check.
- Full Common Practice verification passed: 230 tests across 50 files, plus all
  required build, formatting, lint, type, Effect, unused-code and docs checks.
- Native Alchemy deployed Preview, then production. Each public suite passed
  all eight tests. Independent provider readback and hosted browser checks are

## Caching

The Website's TanStack router preloads links on hover, focus or touch and treats
loaded and preloaded page data as fresh for one minute. Returning to the same
page during that minute reuses its loader data without another page-data
request. Unused data keeps TanStack's default five-minute retention window.
After freshness expires, a return can display the saved data while checking
for an update. A full reload starts a new router cache. These settings live in
`apps/web/src/router.tsx`, not Vite's build configuration.

The minute starts when the loader data was produced. Cloudflare-cached HTML
includes the server's saved loader time, so the first return to the initial
page can need a refresh even soon after opening the Website. That new browser
load starts its own freshness window.

The router's memory cache is separate from HTTP caching below. TanStack server
function replies remain `no-store`; the router can still reuse their returned
data. A returned error envelope is also loader data and can be reused during
the same minute. Browser analytics sends have their own lifecycle.

`@common-practice/http/publishing-policy` supplies the shared cache and safety headers and
API-catalogue Link. It is a pure function over response facts. Both native API
responses and TanStack responses use it; failures and cookie-setting responses
stay `no-store`.

The Website uses native Workers Cache scoped to its Worker version. Successful
anonymous HTML, public Markdown and images make browsers recheck (`max-age=0`), while
Cloudflare may reuse them for seven days. Discovery text and the MCP card have
a five-minute browser lifetime. `Vary: Accept` separates HTML and Markdown
negotiation. Public page API successes follow the same headers; API-catalogue,
OpenAPI, RPC, MCP and failures remain `no-store`. The API does not declare native
Workers Cache; its HTTP headers and isolate image cache have separate roles.
Static assets use Cloudflare's asset cache.

TanStack HTML additionally varies on the complete request Cookie header, so an
anonymous cached response cannot match a saved-appearance request. Responses
with the appearance cookie, including malformed values, use `private, no-store`
and CDN `no-store`. Other cookies can reduce anonymous HTML cache reuse. The
independent machine representations and assets keep their existing rules.
